summary: This RFC describes using the Kerberos pre-authentication framework to carry out one-time password (OTP) authentication, so a client can prove itself with a code that works once.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of a password you reuse, you type in a code that only works one time. This lets Kerberos accept such codes.

questions: how does kerberos otp pre-authentication work
what is the difference between four-pass and two-pass otp
subtitle: How a Kerberos client proves who it is with a code that works only once, instead of a reusable password.

tldr.problem: Kerberos normally relies on a password the user types again and again. Many sites hand out OTP tokens instead, and Kerberos needed a standard way to accept the codes those tokens produce without using the user's Kerberos password.
tldr.mechanism: The OTP value (or a hash of it) is mixed with the FAST Armor Key to make two keys. The client uses one to encrypt a KDC nonce or a timestamp, and the KDC uses the other to encrypt its reply, so both sides prove themselves.
tldr.outcome: Kerberos gets a generic OTP factor with four-pass and two-pass variants, PIN change and resynchronization support. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6560 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) published in April 2012, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
RFC 6560 describes a FAST factor that lets One-Time Password (OTP) values be used in Kerberos V5 pre-authentication, without using the user's Kerberos password. It builds on the pre-authentication framework in RFC 6113 and on Kerberos itself in RFC 4120.

The design is meant to work with different kinds of OTP algorithms: time-based ones, counter-based tokens such as RFC 4226, and challenge-response systems such as RFC 2289. It also covers tokens that plug into the user's computer, for example over USB.

The factor provides three FAST facilities: client-authentication, replacing-reply-key and KDC-authentication. It does not provide strengthening-reply-key. Implementations SHOULD offer a way, such as a provider interface, to add or remove support for a particular OTP mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people carry a small gadget that shows a new number every so often. This document teaches Kerberos to accept those numbers as proof that it really is you.

sections.title: Four-Pass and Two-Pass Exchanges
sections.content:
In the four-pass variant the client sends an initial AS-REQ. If the KDC decides OTP authentication is required, it answers with a KRB-ERROR carrying a PA-OTP-CHALLENGE that includes a random nonce. The client generates the OTP value, encrypts the nonce and returns it in a second AS-REQ inside a PA-OTP-REQUEST. The KDC then replies with the AS-REP.

In the two-pass variant the client skips the challenge. It encrypts a timestamp instead of a nonce and sends the PA-OTP-REQUEST in the very first AS-REQ. The client can do this only when it already knows that the KDC supports OTP pre-authentication, which OTP key to use and the encryption parameters the KDC needs.

All of this travels inside the encrypted tunnel that FAST sets up with an Armor Key. The challenge is carried in the enc-fast-rep of a PA-FX-FAST-REPLY, and the response in the enc-fast-req of a PA-FX-FAST-REQUEST.

When the KDC verifies the request, it uses the AS-REP, encrypted under the newly generated Reply Key, to confirm that it knows the key too. The client MUST NOT continue if it cannot decrypt that reply.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a secret handshake. Either the guard first asks you a question and you answer with your code, or you walk up and show the code with the time stamped on it straight away. Then the guard proves back that he is the real guard.

sections.title: Generating the Client Key and Reply Key
sections.content:
Both sides need two keys. The Client Key encrypts the data in the request (and the KDC decrypts it). The Reply Key is used in the normal way by the KDC to encrypt the AS-REP. Both get the same encryption type as the Armor Key.

How they are made depends on whether the OTP value is sent to the KDC. If the OTP value travels in the otp-value field, both keys are simply the Armor Key. Otherwise they are derived with the KRB-FX-CF2 function from RFC 6113: the first input key is the Armor Key, and the second key, K2, is derived from the OTP value using string-to-key. The four fixed octet strings are the ASCII text OTPComb1 to OTPComb4.

If the KDC can only see hashed OTPs, the client computes H = hash(realm|nonce|OTP) and hashes the result a total of iterationCount times before encoding it for string-to-key. In that case the client picks the first hash algorithm in the KDC's list that it supports, and it MUST NOT use an iteration count lower than the one requested.

Mixing in the Armor Key also ties the inner OTP exchange to the outer FAST tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Your one-time code and a secret already shared by the tunnel are stirred together to bake two new keys, like mixing two paints to get a colour neither paint had alone.

sections.title: Challenge, Request and PIN Messages
sections.content:
Three new pre-authentication data types are defined, each DER-encoded and described in ASN.1.

  • PA-OTP-CHALLENGE (141): the KDC's nonce, an optional otp-service, one or more OTP-TOKENINFO entries, and optional salt and s2kparams values.
  • PA-OTP-REQUEST (142): flags, the encrypted data (encData), and optional hash algorithm, iteration count, OTP value, PIN and hints such as otp-time and otp-counter.
  • PA-OTP-PIN-CHANGE (144): flags, an optional new PIN, length limits, expiry information and a format.

Each OTP-TOKENINFO carries flags that steer the client: nextOTP, combine, collect-pin, do-not-collect-pin, must-encrypt-nonce, separate-pin-required and check-digit. It can also name the vendor, a challenge, the OTP length and format, a token ID, an algorithm URI, and the supported hash algorithms with a minimum iteration count. Support for SHA-256 by both client and KDC is REQUIRED.

If the must-encrypt-nonce flag is set, the OTP value MUST be used for key generation and MUST NOT be sent in otp-value. If it is not set, the OTP value MUST be sent in otp-value and MUST NOT be used for key derivation.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are forms with boxes to fill in. One form is the question from the server, one is your answer, and one is for changing your PIN. Little tick boxes tell your gadget how to behave.

sections.title: PIN Changes, Resynchronization and Errors
sections.content:
Most OTP tokens combine a Personal Identification Number (PIN) with the token's value. If the KDC finds that the PIN has expired, it SHOULD answer with a KRB-ERROR of type KDC_ERR_PIN_EXPIRED and MAY add a PA-OTP-PIN-CHANGE with formatting information. The KDC can also use that message to report a PIN it changed for the user, or to tell the client when the current PIN expires.

Time-based and event-based tokens can drift out of step with the server. The KDC MAY then return a challenge with a single otp-tokenInfo having the nextOTP flag set. The client SHOULD retry with an OTP generated from the next token state, such as the next time interval or counter value, and it MUST set nextOTP in the new request.

The document defines four error codes, and the KDC MUST fail the request with the matching one in these cases.
sections.plainLanguage: If your PIN is too old, the server asks you to pick a new one. If your gadget and the server have lost count of where they are, the server asks you to try the next code.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the OTP exchange is tunneled in a FAST Armor channel, a compromised outer tunnel could allow a man-in-the-middle attack. Using the Armor Key when deriving the inner keys gives crypto-binding to the outer channel. Unless the KDC's identity has been verified, anonymous PKINIT SHALL NOT be used with OTP algorithms that require the OTP value to be sent to the KDC.

The four-pass exchange is a challenge-response protocol, so it uses different keys to encrypt the client and server nonces to help against reflection attacks. A large iteration count could be used for denial of service, so the KDC should reject iteration counts above a maximum set by local policy.

In four-pass mode the KDC can detect replay because the client encrypts a KDC-generated nonce. Two-pass mode encrypts a timestamp and so needs another mechanism, such as an OTP server or a timestamp-based replay cache on the KDC. A hostile KDC might brute-force a short OTP, and a high iteration count can make that infeasible within the OTP's lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel is like a sealed tube for your code. The rules make sure a crook cannot swap the tube, replay an old code, or make the server do endless homework.

sections.title: Registered Values
sections.content:
The OTP algorithm identifier URIs used in otp-algID were registered in the PSKC algorithm registry. The pre-authentication types PA-OTP-CHALLENGE (141), PA-OTP-REQUEST (142) and PA-OTP-PIN-CHANGE (144) are recorded in the registry created by RFC 6113. PA-OTP-CONFIRM (143) is marked OBSOLETE.

The error codes and the key usage value are not managed by IANA at the time of writing, although the RFC notes work in progress to create registries for them.
sections.plainLanguage: The numbers for the new message types are written in an official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

messages.label: AS-REQ
messages.note: Initial request, possibly with other pre-authentication data.

messages.label: KRB-ERROR + PA-OTP-CHALLENGE
messages.note: Carries a random nonce and token information.

messages.label: AS-REQ + PA-OTP-REQUEST
messages.note: The nonce encrypted under the Client Key.

messages.label: AS-REP
messages.note: Encrypted with the Reply Key, which confirms the KDC.

items.label: KDC_ERR_INVALID_HASH_ALG
items.desc: Hash algorithm missing or against KDC policy.

items.label: KDC_ERR_INVALID_ITERATION_COUNT
items.desc: Iteration count against policy or below the challenge value.

items.label: KDC_ERR_PIN_EXPIRED
items.desc: The user's PIN has expired and must change.

items.label: KDC_ERR_PIN_REQUIRED
items.desc: A separate PIN is required but no otp-pin was sent.
